title: Blind against blind
summary: Everyone folds to the small blind: the widest ranges and the small blind’s missing position.

spot.text: Everyone folds to the small blind. Ranges here are the widest: nobody has shown strength, and the small blind plays against one player only. But after the flop the small blind is **out of position**, the main drawback of the spot.

sb.text:
Two approaches for the small blind:
- **Raise or fold**: open 2.5–3 BB with about 40–50% of hands. Simple and aggressive, good against a passive big blind.
- **Limp with a wide range**, plus raises with strong hands and some bluffs. Cheaper, but harder to play after the flop; against an aggressive big blind the limps often get raised.

bb.text: As the big blind against a small blind raise you have **position** on every street and good pot odds, so defend very wide and 3-bet more: the small blind opens wide. Against a small blind limp **raise often**: an iso-raise to 3–4 BB with strong hands and some weak ones that want a fold.

q-k9.q: The small blind limps, you are in the big blind with K9o. What is usually best?
options: Check and fold to any bet
q-k9.explain: K9o is well ahead of a wide limping range, and you have position after the flop.

t1.q: The small blind’s main drawback in blind against blind:
options: It is out of position after the flop
t1.explain: Every postflop street it acts first.

t2.q: How does the big blind play against a small blind raise?
t2.explain: Position and pot odds make a wide defense profitable.

t3.q: The small blind’s "raise or fold" strategy is…
options: Opening about 40–50% of hands without limps
t3.explain: Every hand it plays, it plays with a raise.
